# Data and methods

## Estimand and unit of analysis

We estimate each reform's annual effects on federal revenue and the trust funds
from 2026 through 2100. Let $i$ index households, $y$ index calendar years,
$w_{iy}$ denote the calibrated household weight for year $y$, and $P_0$ and
$P_s$ denote current law and reform scenario $s$. We report the static revenue
effect of scenario $s$ in year $y$ as

$$
\Delta^{static}_{sy}
= \sum_i w_{iy} R_i(P_s, D_{iy}) - \sum_i w_{iy} R_i(P_0, D_{iy}),
$$

where $D_{iy}$ denotes the projected household record and $R_i(\cdot)$ the
PolicyEngine federal income-tax liability calculation. We compute trust-fund
effects the same way for the OASDI and HI revenue components below. In the
static estimand, we hold the projected population, income, and benefit
distribution fixed within a year and vary only the policy parameters.

For the labor-supply response estimand, we use the same projected data and
baseline but let each reform move labor supply through PolicyEngine's
labor-supply response variables before we measure revenue:

$$
\Delta^{LSR}_{sy}
= \sum_i w_{iy} R_i(P_s, D_{iy}, L_i(P_s))
- \sum_i w_{iy} R_i(P_0, D_{iy}, L_i(P_0)).
$$

The behavioral component $L_i(\cdot)$ covers labor supply alone. We do not
reproject population, wage growth, interest rates, benefit claiming, mortality,
or the Social Security trust-fund balance in response to a reform.

## Base microdata

We build on PolicyEngine's populace 2024 household database
(`populace-us-2024-9f1260b-20260611`). PolicyEngine assembles populace from the
CPS Annual Social and Economic Supplement [@census2024cpsasec], the IRS Public
Use File, the Survey of Consumer Finances, the Survey of Income and Program
Participation, the CPS Outgoing Rotation Group, the Medical Expenditure Panel
Survey, and the American Community Survey. It traces every imputed layer to its
source [@peusdata]. We then apply PolicyEngine's federal income-tax,
payroll-tax, Social Security benefit-taxation, and benefit-program rules to each
record.

The projection stores its weights on household records, so the projection and
scoring code aggregates by household. Benefit taxation depends on each tax
unit's filing status, combined income, Social Security benefits, and other
income, and PolicyEngine maps person- and tax-unit-level variables like these to
households before calibration or national aggregation.

## Long-run projection

We build each projection year independently from the same 2024 populace
cross-section, in four stages. Demographics enter through the household weights,
and economics enter through the record values.

**Stage A: grow incomes to the target year.** We uprate each income category
from 2024 to year $y$. Through 2034, we follow the long-term projections of
the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) in PolicyEngine's parameters. After
2034, we cap any category whose cumulative growth would outrun the Trustees'
nominal-GDP path at that path, so no income source grows faster than the
projected economy. We index tax parameters as statute does, with the threshold
treatment we describe below.

**Stage B: reweight to the projected age distribution.** We shift household
weights to the projected single-year age distribution with a light
positive-entropy adjustment. At this stage the weights carry population level
and age structure only.

**Stage C: calibrate values, given those weights.** Holding the reweighted
population fixed, we align the economic aggregates with the Trustees' targets
through three scalars. We scale earnings by $\alpha$ so that taxable payroll,
the wages and self-employment income under the Social Security payroll-tax cap,
matches the Trustees' projection. We scale Social Security benefits by $\beta$
so that they match Trustees OASDI cost, and beneficiary households' income other
than earnings and benefits by $\gamma$ toward the Trustees' taxation-of-benefits
target. Because the 85 percent inclusion cap saturates at the far horizon, total
taxation of benefits barely responds to other income there. We therefore bound
$\gamma$ and let the final calibration close any remainder.

**Stage D: final entropy calibration.** We adjust the weights a final time so
that they hit the age distribution and every fiscal target. We also target
ordinary non-payroll income and preferential investment income at their Stage A
growth paths, so the reweighting cannot inflate income to reach a revenue
target.

Reweighting alone can match dollar aggregates only by changing the population's
makeup, and value scaling alone cannot shift the age structure, so we use each
for its own channel. We take the fiscal targets from the 2026 Social Security
Trustees' current-law projections [@ssa2026trustees] and the HI
taxation-of-benefits target from the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report
[@medicare2026trustees].

We follow two parts of the Trustees' treatment of tax parameters. First, we keep
the Social Security benefit-tax combined-income thresholds fixed in nominal
dollars, as the law sets them and as the Trustees' taxation-of-benefits method
holds them. Second, we index income-tax parameters as current law does through
2034. From 2035, the Trustees assume that income-tax brackets rise with
average wages rather than chained CPI-U, to avoid indefinite bracket compression
relative to income levels [@ssa2026trustees]. The Trustees Report names
income-tax brackets. In May 2026, the Office of the Chief Actuary (OACT) at the
Social Security Administration (SSA) confirmed to PolicyEngine that the same
long-range assumption applies to federal income-tax thresholds such as standard
deductions.[^oact-threshold-email] From 2035, we therefore index the core
federal income-tax thresholds to wages: ordinary income-tax brackets, standard
deductions, the additional standard deduction for aged and blind filers,
capital-gains thresholds, and alternative minimum tax (AMT) thresholds. We keep
other federal income-tax parameters, such as credit amounts and refundability
limits, on current-law indexing unless a reform changes them directly.

For reform parameters outside current law, we follow CRFB's specification on
indexing. For example, we hold the $700 credit's phase-out thresholds at
$150,000 for joint filers and $75,000 for other filers. As a nonrefundable
credit, it reduces no revenue from tax units that owe no income tax before
credits.

| Assumption area | Trustees Report | OACT correspondence | Our implementation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Social Security benefit-tax combined-income thresholds | The Trustees' taxation-of-benefits method holds the statutory thresholds fixed in nominal dollars. | We stated this understanding to OACT, and OACT's reply does not contradict it. | We hold them fixed in nominal dollars, as current law does. |
| Ordinary income-tax brackets | After the tenth projection year, brackets rise with average wages rather than chained CPI-U. | OACT confirmed brackets as part of the long-range assumption. | We index them to wages from 2035. |
| Standard deduction and related deduction thresholds | The report's paragraph on this assumption does not name them. | OACT confirmed that the long-range assumption covers federal income-tax thresholds, including standard deductions. | We index standard deduction amounts and the aged and blind additions to wages from 2035. |
| Capital-gains and AMT thresholds | The report's paragraph on this assumption does not name them. | We treat them as threshold-like federal income-tax parameters under OACT's clarification. | We index the capital-gains thresholds and the AMT brackets, exemptions, phase-out thresholds, and separate-filing thresholds to wages from 2035. |
| Credit amounts, refundability limits, and other non-threshold parameters | The report's taxation-of-benefits paragraph does not specify them. | OACT's reply does not address them. | We keep them on current-law indexing unless a reform changes them directly. |

[^oact-threshold-email]: Email from SSA Office of the Chief Actuary Actuarial
    Services to PolicyEngine, May 5, 2026, replying to "Clarification on
    Trustees long-run income-tax threshold assumption." OACT wrote that the
    long-range assumption applies to income-tax rate brackets and federal
    income-tax thresholds, with standard deductions as an example.

We store each projected year in an H5 file (HDF5, a common format for large
datasets), which holds that year's household weights and input variables. The
projection script writes a metadata file alongside it with the base dataset,
calibration profile, target source, calibration audit, and validation status.

## Calibration targets

We calibrate household weights to five families of official demographic and
fiscal targets.

**Age distribution.** The household age-composition matrix has 86 columns:
single-year ages 0 through 84 and a top-coded 85+ category. We take the
single-year age shape from SSA's 2024 population projections for the Social
Security area [@ssa2024population]. We rescale it within three groups (under
20, 20 to 64, and 65 and over) so that the group totals match Table V.A3 of the
2026 Trustees Report [@ssa2026trustees].

**OASDI benefits.** We calibrate the weighted total of the household-level
`social_security` variable to the 2026 Trustees' OASDI cost projection
[@ssa2026trustees]. This target fixes the benefit base that the reforms tax and
that the solvency baseline cuts.

**OASDI taxable payroll.** We combine household-level taxable wages and taxable
self-employment income under the Social Security payroll-tax cap and calibrate
the weighted total to the Trustees' taxable-payroll projection
[@ssa2026trustees]. This target sets the wage base for payroll-tax and solvency
comparisons.

**OASDI taxation-of-benefits revenue.** We calibrate the household-level
`tob_revenue_oasdi` variable to the 2026 Trustees' current-law
taxation-of-benefits target, which we derive as the Table IV.B2 income-rate share
of Table VI.G1 taxable payroll. This target sets the Social Security trust funds'
share of baseline benefit-tax revenue.

**HI taxation-of-benefits revenue.** We calibrate the household-level
`tob_revenue_medicare_hi` variable to the HI taxation-of-benefits target in the
expanded tables of the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report, which give annual values
through 2100 [@medicare2026trustees]. This target sets the Medicare trust
fund's share of baseline benefit-tax revenue.

Every projected dataset hits all of its calibration targets. The projection
script stops on any year whose final calibration misses a target by more than
0.01 percent. A baseline manifest lists the SHA-256 hash, a fingerprint of the
file's contents, of each baseline H5 and metadata file. The scoring code stops
when a file differs from its listed hash, and every run behind the results file
made that check.

## Far-horizon contributors

A projection that relied on reweighting alone would have to concentrate weight
on a few households that owe tax on benefits (contributors) to match far-horizon
taxation-of-benefits aggregates, forcing a choice between resting the estimates
on a few records and adding synthetic ones. Because economic
growth enters through record values rather than weights, the population of
taxation-of-benefits contributors stays broad even in 2100, and every record
in every projected dataset comes from a real survey household.

We built the datasets under publication gates, and the projection script stops
on any year that fails one. The gates bound the household weights in every year
and, from 2075, the contributors behind each policy target. For OASDI and HI
taxation-of-benefits contributors, they require at least 1,000 positive
contributors, an effective sample size of at least 50, a top-10 contribution
share of at most 50%, a top-100 share of at most 95%, and a largest
single-contributor share of at most 15%. Every projected dataset meets those
limits, including the years before 2075, and we report the figures in
@sec-validation.

We also track the Trustees' covered-worker and beneficiary counts as
diagnostics, but we do not calibrate to them, or to GDP, average wages, or CPI.
The model does not compute GDP, and these series enter only as projection
inputs, including the growth ceiling after 2034.

## Calibration estimator

We use positive entropy calibration. Let $w_i^0$ be the initial household
weight, $a_i$ be the vector of calibration variables for household $i$, and
$t_y$ be the target vector for year $y$. The estimator chooses strictly positive
weights $w_i$ that solve

$$
\min_{w_i>0}
\sum_i \left[
w_i \log\left(\frac{w_i}{w_i^0}\right) - w_i + w_i^0
\right]
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_i w_i a_i = t_y .
$$

This estimator applies entropy balancing to survey calibration
[@deville1992calibration; @hainmueller2012entropy], and we solve its dual problem
by Newton's method with a line search. With scaled constraints $a_i^*$ and
targets $t_y^*$, the dual implies

$$
w_i(\lambda) = w_i^0 \exp(a_i^{*\prime}\lambda),
$$

and the solver finds $\lambda$ such that
$$
\sum_i w_i(\lambda) a_i^* = t_y^*.
$$

For each year we record the target and achieved value of each fiscal constraint,
the largest error on any constraint including the age bins, the share of positive
weights, the effective sample size, and the top-weight concentration. The entropy
parameterization keeps every weight positive. When exact positive calibration has
no solution on the available survey records, the projection script stops with an
error.

## Policy simulation and trust-fund accounting {#sec-trust-fund-accounting}

For each reform and year, the scoring code loads the calibrated year-$y$
dataset, runs a baseline PolicyEngine simulation and a reform simulation on the
same records, saves the reform simulation in its own H5 file, and stores both
levels and differences. It writes these core output columns:

| Output | Definition |
|---|---|
| `revenue_impact` | Reform minus baseline federal income tax. |
| `tob_oasdi_impact` | Reform minus baseline OASDI taxation-of-benefits revenue. |
| `tob_medicare_hi_impact` | Reform minus baseline HI taxation-of-benefits revenue. |
| `tob_total_impact` | Sum of the OASDI and HI taxation-of-benefits impacts. |
| `oasdi_net_impact` | Net OASDI trust-fund impact after reform-specific gains and losses. |
| `hi_net_impact` | Net HI trust-fund impact after reform-specific gains and losses. |

How we credit revenue to the trust funds depends on the reform and the split.
For most reforms, the dashboard's default split divides revenue between OASDI
and HI by each fund's share of baseline benefit-tax revenue, and the headline
summary (@sec-headline) uses that split. The trust-fund decomposition in
@sec-results instead uses the model's OASDI and HI taxation-of-benefits
variables. Senior-deduction and credit changes can move federal income tax by
more than they move the trust funds' revenue. For the senior-deduction repeal,
total revenue equals the full federal income-tax impact, while OASDI, HI, and
general-fund columns show the accounting split. A reform can therefore raise
income-tax revenue while it weakens one trust fund, or replace benefit-tax
revenue with employer-contribution revenue that splits differently between OASDI
and HI.

### Trust-fund accounting for the Roth swaps {#sec-swap-accounting}

For the Roth swap and the phased Roth swap, we credit each trust fund with the
income tax on its own employer contribution: the employer Social Security
contribution funds OASDI, and the employer Medicare contribution funds HI. For
each tax unit, we compute income tax with both employer contributions in income,
compute it again with one fund's contribution removed, and credit the difference
to that fund, with a floor of zero. For the short phase-in Roth before 2033, we
pool the two gains. We credit OASDI first, up to its 6.2 of the 7.65 percentage
points of employer payroll tax, and HI with the rest. We then subtract the
benefit-tax revenue each fund loses to get its net impact.

We measure each gain as if its own contribution were the last income taxed, so
the two gains need not add up to the income tax on both contributions together.
The two funds' net impacts therefore need not sum to the change in federal
income tax. In our results the sums exceed that change in every year: over
2026-2035, by $12.7 billion for the Roth swap, $36.2 billion for the phased Roth
swap, and $24.5 billion for the short phase-in Roth, and by $11.8 billion for
each in 2100. We report the sum of the two funds' net impacts on the dashboard
and in the headline summary (@sec-headline), and the change in federal income
tax in the revenue tables of @sec-results.

## Anchor years

We run the full microsimulation for every reform in a set of anchor years and
interpolate linearly between them. The anchors include 2026, 2030, and every
fifth year from 2035 through 2100, plus the years below where reform
schedules bend. Each row of the public results file records whether it comes
from an anchor-year simulation (an exact anchor) or from interpolation, and we
sum the complete annual series for the long-run and present-value totals.

Linear interpolation tracks a reform's annual impact where that impact changes
smoothly, but it misses a sharp change between anchors. In the 2025
reconciliation act, Congress created several temporary deductions that apply
through 2028, among them the bonus senior deduction and deductions for tips,
overtime pay, and auto-loan interest. It also raised the cap on the
state-and-local-tax deduction through 2029. The impact of a reform that
interacts with those provisions jumps within the budget window, and a straight
line from 2026 to 2030 cannot follow the jump. For example, the senior-deduction
repeal changes only the bonus senior deduction, which expires after 2028 under
current law, so the reform's impact falls to zero in 2029. A straight line
between the 2026 and 2030 anchors would understate its 2028 impact by $9.9
billion.

We add exact anchors where the schedules bend. We scanned every model parameter
that changes discretely between 2027 and 2034 and found no other federal
discontinuity that matters for these reforms. Exact anchors in 2028 and 2029,
for every reform, bracket both changes. The short phase-in Roth raises the
taxable share of employer payroll tax each year until it reaches 100 percent in
2033, so we add exact anchors in 2032 and 2033 at that corner. The phased Roth
swap phases benefit taxation out in a straight line that ends in 2062, between
the 2060 and 2065 anchors, so we add an exact anchor in 2062. Once its phase-out
ends, the phased Roth swap reaches the Roth swap's settings, so we also score
the Roth swap in 2062, and the two exact scores agree to the dollar. Straight
lines between the 2060 and 2065 anchors would put them $19.5 billion apart. The
Roth swap and the reverse Roth take full effect at once and need no further
anchors.

## Solvency-baseline scoring

We also score four reforms against a Social Security solvency baseline: full
repeal, 85 percent taxation, 100 percent taxation, and the phased Roth swap. In
each scored year from 2035, we bring the program into annual balance on that
year's calibrated dataset with a balanced "traditional fix" in two stages, then
apply the reform:

1. **Benefit reduction.** We cut every benefit by a uniform multiplier, enough
   to close half of the gap between that year's OASDI income and scheduled
   benefits.
2. **Payroll-rate increase.** We close the remaining OASDI gap with equal
   employee and employer OASDI rate increases. We close the HI gap with equal
   employee and employer HI rate changes, cutting both rates in years when HI
   runs a surplus.

Before scoring any reform, the code checks that both trust-fund gaps close
within tolerance and that the current-law simulation reproduces the published
current-law row for the same year. We then score each reform as a change from
the solvent system, split its revenue by baseline trust-fund shares, and assign
any residual to the general fund. The components of every row sum to the total.

We simulate the solvency baseline in 2035, 2050, 2065, 2075, and 2100.
In 2065, the phased Roth swap's OASDI and HI impacts run $32.7 billion and
$41.1 billion below a straight line between 2050 and 2075. Between anchors, we
interpolate the rows themselves linearly rather than the ratio of solvent to
current-law results, which diverges where current-law totals cross zero, as the
phased Roth swap's do. Before 2035, the solvency fix leaves current law
unchanged, so we score those years against scheduled benefits and the series
runs from 2026 to 2100.

## Present-value convention {#sec-present-value}

We discount each year's flow to the start of 2026 at each trust fund's
effective interest rates under the Trustees' intermediate assumptions. For OASDI
flows, we use the annual effective yields that the compound effective trust-fund
interest factors in Table VI.G1 of the 2026 OASDI Trustees Report imply
[@ssa2026trustees]. SSA uses the reciprocals of those factors as discount
factors for summarized rates and balances. For HI flows, we use the effective
rates in Table IV.A4 of the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report through 2035
[@medicare2026trustees]. As that table does, we then grade them linearly to the
4.7 percent ultimate nominal rate by 2040 and hold them constant after that.
We discount general-fund flows and economy-wide denominators (taxable payroll
and GDP) with the OASDI series and sum the discounted components into the
75-year total, so headline figures add up across trust funds. For ten-year
totals, we sum nominal flows over 2026-2035.

## Supplemental labor-supply response scoring {#sec-labor-supply}

We show static estimates on the dashboard and report labor-supply response rows
in the public results file as a secondary estimand. We simulate them on the same
projected datasets as the static rows, save each reform's H5 file, and aggregate
from those files. We score labor-supply responses for thirteen of the fifteen
reforms, all but full MAGI inclusion and the 2005 Tax Panel deduction, and for
the short phase-in Roth. For each, we simulate 2026 and 2100, plus 2062 for the
Roth swap and the phased Roth swap and 2033 for the short phase-in Roth. Between
these anchors, we interpolate each metric's ratio of labor-supply to static
results linearly and apply it to the static annual row. Where the static result
changes sign within a segment, we interpolate the labor-supply values directly.

For each labor-supply run, we combine the reform's statutory parameters with our
age-based elasticity schedule:

- income elasticity base: -0.05
- income elasticity multiplier above the model's older-worker threshold: 2.0
- primary-earner substitution elasticities by decile: 0.31, 0.28, 0.27,
  0.27, 0.25, 0.25, 0.22, 0.22, 0.22, and 0.22
- secondary-earner substitution elasticity: 0.27
- substitution elasticity multiplier above the older-worker threshold: 2.0

We double the older-worker elasticities because the studies we review below find
that near-retirement and retirement-age workers respond more on the labor-supply
margin than prime-age workers. We estimate partial-equilibrium revenue effects
under that schedule, without macroeconomic feedback.

### Empirical basis for the older-worker multiplier

We apply the age adjustment as one multiplier on both elasticities at age 65
and over, rather than as a full age-by-decile schedule. Studies find higher
responsiveness at older ages but offer no breakdown by age and income decile,
and one multiplier stays easy to vary in sensitivity analysis. We base the values
under 65 on CBO's working-paper reviews: substitution (Frisch)
elasticities of 0.27--0.53 with a 0.40 central value [@reichlingwhalen2012] and
income elasticities of $-0.02$ to $-0.05$ [@mcclellandmok2012]. @keane2011
surveys the wider range.

For older workers, structural and reduced-form estimates imply substitution
elasticities two to three times the prime-age values. @french2005 estimates
elasticities rising from 0.2--0.4 at age 40 to 1.0--1.3 by age 60 in a
life-cycle model (roughly $3\times$). @blaushvydko2011 find extensive-margin
elasticities of 0.5--0.8 at ages 62--69 against intensive-margin values of
0.05--0.2 (roughly $2$--$3\times$). @coilegruber2007 estimate 0.4--0.7 at ages
62--64 from Social Security entitlement variation (roughly $2\times$), and
@gustmansteinmeier2009 estimate 0.45--0.8 at ages 65--69 from pension--Social
Security interactions ($2$--$2.5\times$). On the income side, @french2005 and
@gustmansteinmeier2009 imply elasticities of $-0.06$ to $-0.10$ for workers 60
and over against the $-0.04$ prime-age central value ($1.5$--$2\times$). The
life-cycle calibration in @rogersonwallenius2009 supports a similar ratio. Our
multiplier of 2.0 for both elasticities sits at the low end of these ranges, and
a range of 1.5 to 3.0 spans the estimates. Most of the evidence on older workers
identifies the extensive margin, while PolicyEngine applies elasticities to
total earnings, so the multiplier carries participation responses into
earnings. Older cohorts in far-horizon years may also differ from the
estimation samples in assets, defined-benefit pension coverage, and health, so
the multiplier reflects today's evidence rather than a forecast for future
cohorts.

## Limitations

The base microdata come from surveys and carry sampling error, item
nonresponse, and imputation error. We calibrate to selected aggregate margins,
not to the full joint distribution of age, earnings, Social Security benefits,
filing status, health spending, and assets. We take long-run HI expenditures
from the Trustees as an external denominator on the dashboard rather than
microsimulating HI spending. The labor-supply estimates depend on our elasticity
choices and omit macroeconomic feedback, portfolio responses, claiming
responses, mortality changes, and political responses to trust-fund exhaustion.
